summary: Chinese greetings and polite words are fixed formulas that never change their form. The one choice to make is 你 or 您: 您好 for elders, teachers, customers and strangers to be respected, 你好 between equals. In daily life Chinese greet less with ‘hello’ than with a name or title (老师好！, 王老师！) or a friendly question (吃了吗？ ‘have you eaten?’); 你好吗 ‘how are you?’ is a real question for people you have not seen for a while. There is no form for ‘to a man’ or ‘to a woman’.

blocks.caption: The formulas of this lesson

items.title: 你 nǐ
points: people of your age in casual settings

items.title: 您 nín
points: strangers you want to respect — especially in the north

blocks.title: 你好吗 is rarer than textbooks suggest
blocks.text: As a daily greeting 你好吗 sounds like a textbook. Friends say 最近怎么样？ ‘how have you been?’ or greet with a name or 吃了吗？.

blocks.title: Excuse me — which one?
blocks.text: 打扰一下 to interrupt or ask; 不好意思 the everyday light ‘excuse me / sorry’; 请问 right before a question; 劳驾 (northern, a bit old-fashioned) or 借过 / 让一下 to get past.

blocks.title: Sorry is two words
blocks.text: 对不起 is a real apology; 不好意思 is for small things — bumping into someone, being late by a minute, asking a favour. The answer to both is 没关系 ‘never mind’.

blocks.title: Names
blocks.text: Chinese names start with the surname: 王小明 is Mr Wang. 我叫王小明 gives the whole name; 我姓王 ‘my surname is Wang’. Politely ask an elder: 您贵姓？

askYourself: Who am I talking to — an equal, or someone older, a teacher, a customer? → 你好 or 您好.
Is it morning, evening, or am I leaving at night? → 早上好 / 晚上好 / 晚安.
Do I know when we will meet again? → time + 见 (明天见); if not → 回头见 or 再见.
Have we not seen each other for a while? → 你好吗？ (or 最近怎么样？)
Am I apologizing for something real, or just interrupting? → 对不起 or 不好意思 / 打扰一下.
Do I want someone to do something? → 请 + verb, before the verb.
steps: Pick the formula for the situation.
Add a name or title if you know it: 老师好, 王老师，您好.

traps: *你们好 to a teacher — say 老师好 or 您好.
请 at the end of the request: *坐，请 → 请坐 (请 always stands before the verb).
Answering 谢谢 with 没关系 (that is for apologies) — say 不客气.
晚安 as an evening greeting — it means ‘good night’; greet with 晚上好.
Using 拜拜 with your boss — 再见 is safer.

quiz.q: You meet your teacher in the morning. What do you say?
quiz.why: Title + 早上好; 晚安 is for the night, 拜拜 too casual.

quiz.q: Someone says 谢谢. You answer:
quiz.why: 没关系 answers an apology, not thanks.

quiz.q: You bump into someone on the bus. The most natural word:
quiz.why: A light ‘sorry’ for a small thing.

quiz.q: Where does 请 go in ‘Please sit down’?
Which greeting is rarer in real life than in textbooks?
quiz.why: It is used mainly after not seeing each other for a while.
叫 is the verb ‘to be called’ — no 是.

quiz.q: You’ll see your friend tomorrow. You say:
quiz.why: Time word + 见 = see you then.

notes.text: Γεια σου / γεια σας ↔ 你好 / 您好: Greek, too, builds the polite ‘you’ into the greeting. But γεια serves for hello and goodbye, while Chinese parts with 再见; and παρακαλώ is both ‘please’ and ‘you’re welcome’, which Chinese splits into 请 and 不客气.

Привет / Здравствуйте ↔ 你好 / 您好 — the polite ‘you’ is in the greeting. Пожалуйста is ‘please’ and ‘you’re welcome’; Chinese splits it into 请 (before the verb) and 不客气. Respect comes from name and patronymic in Russian, from surname + title in Chinese (王老师).

Hola has no polite form; Chinese chooses 你好 or 您好. Por favor may close a request (un café, por favor); 请 must open it (请坐). Buenas noches greets and parts at night, but Chinese 晚安 only parts — the evening greeting is 晚上好.

English hello and please have no polite form; Chinese marks respect with 您好. ‘Please’ can end an English request, 请 cannot (请等我). ‘Good night’ is a parting in both languages (晚安); ‘good evening’ is 晚上好.
Bonjour / bonsoir work for anyone; Chinese picks 你好 or 您好 as you pick tu or vous. S’il vous plaît closes a request, 请 opens it (请进). Bonne nuit ↔ 晚安: for parting only.
Hallo and Guten Tag carry no du / Sie, but 你好 / 您好 do. Bitte is ‘please’ and ‘you’re welcome’; Chinese has 请 (before the verb) and 不客气. Auf Wiedersehen and 再见 are built alike: 再 ‘again’ + 见 ‘see’.

नमस्ते works at any hour, for hello and goodbye; Chinese changes with the time of day (早上好, 晚上好) and parts with 再见. Hindi shows respect in the verb (बैठिए ‘please sit’) and with आप; Chinese with 请 + verb (请坐) and 您.
Persian salām / khodāhāfez ↔ 你好 / 再见; respect shows in shomā and in polite verb forms, in Chinese in 您 and 请. Persian lotfan ‘please’ can open or close a request; 请 only stands before the verb.
नमस्कार serves for hello and goodbye at any hour; Chinese greets with 你好 / 您好 and parts with 再见. Marathi respect lies in तुम्ही / आपण and the verb; Chinese respect in 您, 请 and titles.

Arabic greetings have fixed answers (as-salāmu ʿalaykum — wa-ʿalaykumu s-salām) and many change for a man or a woman (kayfa ḥāluka / ḥāluki). Chinese formulas never change: 你好 is answered with 你好, and the only choice is 你 or 您.

Shalom is hello and goodbye; Chinese has 你好 and 再见. Hebrew ‘how are you’ depends on gender (ma shlomkha / ma shlomekh); 你好吗 does not. Bevakasha is both ‘please’ and ‘you’re welcome’; Chinese uses 请 and 不客气.

Merhaba has no sen / siz form; Chinese chooses 你好 or 您好. Lütfen may follow the request (bir çay lütfen); 请 only precedes the verb. Turkish names put the given name first; Chinese names put the surname first (王小明).

Like Japanese, Chinese puts the family name first (王小明, like 山田太郎) and greets people by title (老师好). But Chinese has no humble or honorific verb forms: politeness is 您, 请 and the title, and the verb stays the same.
Korean shows politeness with speech levels in every verb ending; Chinese has none: 您, 请, titles (王老师) and phrases like 您贵姓 do that work, and the verb never changes. Both put the family name first.
Finnish moi / hei / terve are neutral; Chinese chooses 你好 or 您好. Kiitos ↔ 谢谢; ole hyvä is ‘you’re welcome’ and also ‘here you are’ — Chinese answers thanks with 不客气 and offers with 请 (请喝茶).
Hungarian, like Chinese, puts the family name first (Kovács János ~ 王小明). Szia / jó napot kívánok ↔ 你好 / 您好 — a casual and a respectful greeting; köszönöm ↔ 谢谢, szívesen ↔ 不客气.
Swahili greetings are exchanges with set answers (Habari? — Nzuri; to an elder Shikamoo — Marahaba). Chinese has a respectful 您好 for elders but no fixed answer word: 你好 is answered with 你好.
Luganda greetings are exchanges with set replies (Oli otya? — Bulungi), often several turns long. Chinese greetings are short fixed formulas; respect is shown with 您 and titles (王老师好).

Xin chào ↔ 你好, cảm ơn ↔ 谢谢, and Vietnamese, like Chinese, puts the family name first (Nguyễn Văn An). But Vietnamese adds a kinship word to every greeting (chào anh, chào bác), where Chinese uses 您 or a title.
Inuktitut greetings are verb words with person endings (Qanuippit? ‘how are you?’); Chinese greetings are fixed formulas that never change. Qujannamiik ↔ 谢谢.

seeAlso.note: Arabic greetings have fixed replies (as-salāmu ʿalaykum — wa-ʿalaykumu s-salām) and many change for a man or a woman (kayfa ḥāluka / ḥāluki); Chinese formulas never change — only 你 / 您.
Hebrew shalom is both hello and goodbye, and ‘how are you’ depends on gender (ma shlomkha / ma shlomekh); Chinese has no gender in address.
German du / Sie ↔ 你 / 您: both mark respect, but Sie is the default with any adult stranger, while many younger Chinese use 你 with strangers of their own age.
